_note: Hand-written, checked against data/sections.jsonl by src/playbooks.py. 'law' steps cite a section in the corpus; 'general' steps are common practical guidance, not from BNS/BNSS, and are labelled that way in the app. 'priority' orders playbooks when several fire: the more specific situation (police refusal, a false case, custody violence, rape, a missing person) is shown first. 'generic' is the fallback plan: steps true for any offence, attached to whatever sections retrieval finds when no playbook fits.

playbooks.title: Road accident or collision
playbooks.intro: A collision can involve a criminal complaint, a medical record and an insurance claim. Which laws apply depends on whether anyone was hurt and how the other driver behaved.

laws.why: If a driver drove so rashly or negligently that human life was endangered or hurt was likely.
Any rash or negligent act that endangers life or others' safety. It carries a higher punishment if hurt or grievous hurt is caused.
Only if someone died. Sub-section (2), on a driver who causes death by rash driving and escapes without reporting it, has not been brought into force yet (as of mid-2026).

steps.text: Check yourself and others for injury. If anyone is hurt or there is danger, call 112 now (police and ambulance).
Stop. Do not leave the scene. Switch on hazard lights and, if the vehicle can move and nobody is badly hurt, move it out of the traffic.
If you were the driver and someone is hurt, stop, help them and call 112. Leaving the scene makes your position much worse.
Photograph both vehicles, the number plates, the damage, the road and the location. Note the time.
Take the other driver's name, phone number, licence, registration and insurance details, and the names and numbers of witnesses. If they drive off, write down the plate number immediately.

Tell the police. Information about an offence can be given orally or electronically at any police station. It must be written down, read back to you and signed by you, and you are entitled to a copy free of cost. Insurers usually ask for it.
Get medical attention even for minor pain and keep the records and bills.
Inform your insurer promptly and check the time limit in your policy.
If the police refuse to record your information, send it in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, who can investigate or direct an investigation. You can also apply to the Magistrate.

gather: Other driver's details and vehicle number
FIR copy and insurance claim number
playbooks.outside: Insurance claims and compensation for accident victims fall under the Motor Vehicles Act, which is not part of this tool. A lawyer or your insurer can advise on that.
examples: someone rear-ended my car in traffic
a car crashed into my bike
I was in a road accident and the other driver ran away
a drunk driver hit my father, he is in hospital
a bus hit my scooter from behind
I hit a pedestrian with my car

playbooks.title: Theft, snatching or robbery
triggers: \b(?:phone|mobile|laptop|wallet|purse|bag|handbag|cash|money|jewel\w*|gold|watch|bike|car|scooter|cycle|bicycle|ring|necklace|chain|parcel)\b.{0,30}\b(?:went missing|is missing|was missing|missing from|disappeared|is gone|was gone)\b
playbooks.intro: The law treats theft, snatching and robbery differently depending on force and where it happened.

laws.why: Dishonestly taking movable property out of someone's possession without consent.
If the thing was grabbed suddenly or by force, for example a phone or chain snatched on the street.
If someone broke into or secretly entered a house to commit the theft (house-breaking). Higher punishment at night.
If the theft was from a home, a vehicle or a place of worship.
If force, threat or fear was used. That makes it robbery, not theft.
For anyone who knowingly keeps or buys the stolen property.

steps.text: If anyone is in danger or injured, call 112.
Write down what was taken, when and where, and anything you remember about the person. Do not confront them.
If a phone, cards or UPI access were taken, call your bank to block cards and UPI and ask your mobile operator to block the SIM. Note the phone's IMEI number from its box or bill.
Report it at a police station. You can give the information at any police station, irrespective of where the offence happened, orally or electronically.
Ask for the copy of your information. It must be given to you free of cost.
If the police refuse to record it, send the substance in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.

gather: Bill, IMEI or serial number of the item
examples: someone stole my phone
thieves broke into our house at night
my laptop went missing from my room
two men on a bike pulled my gold chain
my car was stolen from the parking lot
I got robbed at knifepoint
my maid has been taking cash from the cupboard

playbooks.title: Cheating or online fraud
triggers: \b(?:used|misused|using|took|stole)\b.{0,15}\b(?:my|our)\b.{0,10}\b(?:aadhaa?r|pan(?: card)?|identity|id proof|kyc|documents?|photos?|name|details|signature)\b.{0,60}\b(?:sim|loan|account|card|profile|to get|to take|to open|without my)\b|\bidentity theft\b
playbooks.intro: Cheating and fraud can be reported to the police, and for online money fraud speed matters because banks can sometimes freeze the money.

laws.why: Deceiving someone to make them hand over money or property, or to do something they would not otherwise do.
If the person pretended to be someone else, including a fake online account in your name.
If you handed something over for safekeeping or a purpose and it was dishonestly used or kept.
If fake documents were made.
If a forged document or electronic record was used as genuine.

steps.text: If money left your account, call your bank at once and ask to freeze or reverse the transaction. For online financial fraud also call the national cyber-crime helpline 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in as soon as possible.

If someone calls claiming a relative is in custody, or that you are under 'digital arrest', and asks for money: do not pay. Police never ask for money on a call. Hang up and call the police station or 112 yourself to check.
Do not delete anything. Take screenshots of chats, profiles, payment receipts, transaction IDs, phone numbers and UPI IDs.
Report it to the police. Information can be given by electronic communication. If you do, it is taken on record once you sign it within three days.
Ask for a copy of what was recorded. It must be given to you free of cost.
If the police refuse, send it in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.

gather: Seller or account details, phone numbers, UPI IDs
playbooks.outside: Hacking and other online-specific offences are in the IT Act, which is not part of this tool. A pure money dispute with no deception from the start (a loan not repaid, say) may be a civil matter.
examples: I was cheated by a fake seller online
I lost money in a UPI scam after sharing an OTP
a fake job offer asked me to pay a registration fee
I invested in a scheme promising double returns and they vanished
someone made a fake account using my photos
someone hacked my email and is asking my friends for money
the documents of the car I bought turned out to be forged
someone called saying my son is arrested and we must pay to release him

playbooks.title: Physical attack or injury
playbooks.intro: The law distinguishes between a simple hurt, a grievous hurt and the use of weapons. A fracture is grievous hurt.

laws.why: Intentionally causing bodily pain, disease or infirmity.
If acid was thrown or used. This carries at least ten years' imprisonment, and the fine goes to the victim's treatment.
Defines grievous hurt, which includes a fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth.
Intentionally causing grievous hurt.
If a weapon or a dangerous means was used.
If you were hit or grabbed but not injured: assault or criminal force.
If an animal attacked you and its owner knew it was dangerous but did not take enough care to guard against the risk.

steps.text: Get to safety and call 112 if you are in danger or hurt. For an acid attack, wash the area with plenty of clean water and get to a hospital at once.
Get medical treatment. Ask the doctor to record how the injury happened. Keep reports, bills and photos of the injuries.
Report it to the police. They must write it down, read it back and have you sign it. You get a copy free of cost.
Minor offences may be non-cognizable. In that case the police only record the information and refer you to the Magistrate, and they cannot investigate without the Magistrate's order.
If the police refuse to record a cognizable offence, send it in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.

gather: Photos of injuries and the place
Messages or calls before or after the incident
examples: my neighbour slapped me during an argument
a group of boys beat up my brother
he hit me with an iron rod and broke my arm
someone pushed me down the stairs and I fractured my hand
someone threw acid on my sister
my neighbour's dog attacked me and they knew it was aggressive

playbooks.title: Threats or blackmail
playbooks.intro: Threats to hurt you, your family, your reputation or your property are covered, and demanding money under threat is a separate and more serious offence.

laws.why: Threatening injury to your person, reputation or property to cause alarm or to make you do something.
If the person is demanding money or something valuable and using the fear of injury or exposure to get it.
If private images are involved, for example pictures of a woman in a private act captured or shared without consent.

steps.text: If you are in immediate danger, call 112.
Do not pay and do not delete anything. Screenshot the messages, call logs, numbers, profiles and payment requests. Record calls only if you can do so lawfully.
For online threats, also report the account to the platform and at cybercrime.gov.in.
Report it to the police. It can be given orally or electronically, it is recorded and signed, and you get a copy free of cost.
If the police do not record it, send it in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.

gather: Phone numbers, profile links, payment requests
Any earlier messages showing the relationship
playbooks.outside: Online blackmail may also involve the IT Act, which is not part of this tool.
examples: someone is threatening to kill me
my ex is threatening to post my private photos unless I pay
a person is blackmailing me
a goon is demanding money from my shop or else
he says he will hurt my family

playbooks.title: Stalking or sexual harassment of a woman
playbooks.intro: These offences are specifically covered, and the law has special rules to make reporting easier for women.

laws.why: Repeatedly following or contacting a woman despite a clear sign of disinterest, or monitoring her online activity.
Unwelcome physical contact, demands for sexual favours, showing pornography or sexual remarks.
Assault or force on a woman intending to outrage her modesty.
Words, gestures or acts intended to insult a woman's modesty.
Capturing or sharing images of a woman in a private act without consent.

steps.text: If you are in danger now, call 112. The Women Helpline numbers 181 and 1091 are also available in many states.
Keep evidence: screenshots, call logs, photos, the person's number, profile and any CCTV locations. Do not delete anything.
When a woman reports offences such as sexual harassment, stalking or outraging her modesty, the information must be recorded by a woman police officer.
You can report at any police station, orally or electronically. It is read back to you, you sign it, and you get a copy free of cost.
If the police refuse, send it in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.
If you fear for your safety as a witness, ask about the witness protection scheme.

gather: Dates and places of each incident
A trusted person who can accompany you to the police station
examples: a man keeps following me and messaging me
a man is sending me vulgar messages
my boss touches me inappropriately
someone secretly recorded me in a trial room
a man exposed himself to me on the bus
my senior makes sexual remarks about me
a boy keeps stalking my daughter

playbooks.title: Cruelty by husband or in-laws, or dowry harassment
triggers: \b(?:in[- ]?laws?|mother[- ]in[- ]law|father[- ]in[- ]law|sister[- ]in[- ]law|brother[- ]in[- ]law|husband'?s (?:family|parents|mother|father|sister|brother))\b.{0,40}\b(?:locked me out|threw me out|thrown out|kept my|took my|taken my|harass\w*|beat\w*|taunt\w*|tortur\w*|abus\w*|hit|slap\w*)
playbooks.intro: Cruelty by a husband or his relatives, including dowry harassment, is a criminal offence. Your safety comes first.

laws.why: A husband or his relative subjecting a woman to cruelty.
Defines cruelty, including wilful conduct that risks serious harm, and harassment to force dowry or property demands.
Dowry death: if a married woman dies within seven years of marriage in unnatural circumstances after dowry-related cruelty.
If you were physically hurt.

steps.text: If you are in danger, call 112 or the Women Helpline 181 and go to a safe place such as a relative's home or a shelter.
Keep medical records, photos of injuries, messages, call records and a list of dowry demands and payments.
Report it at any police station. It is written down, read back and signed by you, and you get a copy free of cost.
If the police do not record it, send it in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.
If you and your children are not being supported, a Magistrate can order monthly maintenance.
Free legal aid is available from your District Legal Services Authority (NALSA helpline 15100).

gather: Marriage proof and list of gifts or payments
Contacts of family or neighbours who saw it
playbooks.outside: Protection orders and the right to stay in the shared home come under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, which is not part of this tool.
examples: my husband beats me every day
my in-laws are demanding more dowry
my husband and his mother torture me
my husband threw me out of the house
the man next door beats his wife

playbooks.title: Police refusing to register a complaint or take action
triggers: \bpolice\b.{0,60}\b(?:no action|haven'?t taken any action|did nothing|not doing anything|ignoring)\b

^(?=.*\b(?:police|station|officers?|SHO|cops?|inspector)\b).*?\b(?:sent me away|turned me away|chased me away|asked me to (?:leave|go away)|without (?:writing|registering|recording|taking|filing) (?:my|the|a) (?:complaint|fir|report))\b
^(?=.*\b(?:police|station|SHO|cops?)\b).*?\bcomplaint\b.{0,60}\b(?:done nothing|no action|nothing happened|no response|not investigat\w*|not acted)\b
playbooks.intro: The police must record information about a cognizable offence. The law gives you steps if they refuse or do nothing.

laws.why: Information about a cognizable offence can be given at any police station, orally or electronically, and must be recorded. Sub-section (4) is your remedy if they refuse.
Sub-section (3) lets a Magistrate order an investigation after considering your application supported by an affidavit.
For non-cognizable offences the police record the information and refer you to the Magistrate.

steps.text: Anyone can give the information, not only the victim, and at any police station, whichever area the offence happened in. Say you want it recorded and ask for the officer in charge.
You can also send it electronically. It is taken on record once you sign it within three days.

For offences punishable by three years or more but less than seven, the police may, with a Deputy Superintendent of Police's permission, do a preliminary enquiry within fourteen days before registering.

If they still refuse, send the substance of your information in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police. If satisfied that it discloses a cognizable offence, the Superintendent shall investigate or direct an investigation.
You can apply to the Magistrate, with an affidavit, who may order an investigation after an inquiry.
Keep a record of who you spoke to, when, and what you were told. Send the written complaint by registered post and keep the receipt.

gather: Copy of your written complaint and the post receipt
Date, time and name or number of the officer
Any evidence of the original offence
playbooks.outside: A lawyer or the District Legal Services Authority (NALSA helpline 15100) can help draft the affidavit and the application.
examples: the police are refusing to file my FIR
I went to the police station but they sent me away
police are not taking any action on my complaint
the police said they won't register a complaint because I'm not the victim

playbooks.title: Arrest or custody (yours or a relative's)
triggers: \bpolice (?:took|took away|have taken|picked up|detained|is holding|are holding|has taken|came and took) (?:my|our) (?:son|daughter|brother|sister|father|dad|mother|mom|husband|wife|friend|cousin|uncle|nephew|boyfriend|girlfriend|relative|neighbou?r)\b
playbooks.intro: A person who is arrested has rights from the moment of arrest, and so does the family.

laws.why: The arrested person must be told the grounds of arrest and, if bailable, that they are entitled to bail.
The police must inform a relative, friend or person nominated by the arrested person, and record who was informed.
The arrested person may meet an advocate of their choice during interrogation.
No more than twenty-four hours in police custody without a Magistrate, excluding travel time.
The arrested person must be examined by a medical officer after arrest, and injuries must be recorded.

steps.text: The arrested person should stay calm, not resist, note the officer's name and station, and not sign blank or unread papers.
Ask for the grounds of arrest. For a bailable offence the person must also be told they can get bail.
Ask the police to inform a family member or friend where the person is being held. Relatives can ask the station for the same information.

The arresting officer must wear a clear name identification and prepare a memorandum of arrest, attested by a witness (a family member or a respectable person of the locality) and countersigned by the arrested person.
The arrested person can ask to meet their lawyer during questioning. If they cannot afford one, ask for free legal aid.
They must be produced before a Magistrate within twenty-four hours (excluding travel time). Only a Magistrate can authorise longer custody.
A medical examination must follow the arrest. Ask for it and tell the doctor about any injury. A copy of the report can go to the arrested person or someone they nominate.
Apply for bail. It is available as of right for bailable offences. For non-bailable offences the court decides.

gather: Name and number of the officer, station name
Time and place of the arrest
examples: my father was arrested by the police yesterday
police picked up my son last night and won't tell us where he is
my brother has been in police custody for two days
the police detained my husband without telling us why

playbooks.title: Bail, or fear of arrest
playbooks.intro: What kind of bail you can get depends on whether the offence is bailable and whether you have already been arrested.

laws.why: Bail for a bailable offence is a right once the person is ready to give bail.
When bail may be granted for a non-bailable offence, and when it may not.
Advance (anticipatory) bail if you expect to be arrested for a non-bailable offence. Apply to the High Court or Sessions Court.
A person who has already been detained for up to half the maximum sentence for the offence while under trial can be released on bail. Different rules apply to the most serious offences.

steps.text: Speak to a criminal lawyer as early as you can. If you cannot afford one, free legal aid is available from the District Legal Services Authority (NALSA helpline 15100).
If the offence is bailable, you can ask for bail from the police or the court right away.
If it is non-bailable, the court decides. Your lawyer applies to the Magistrate or Sessions Court.
If you have not been arrested but expect to be, your lawyer can apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction to release you on bail if you are arrested.
If you have already spent a long time as an under-trial prisoner, ask your lawyer about the maximum detention period.

gather: Court order or arrest memo, if any
examples: how do I get bail for my brother
I am afraid I will be arrested
can I get anticipatory bail
my son is in jail, how do we get him out

playbooks.title: Being held or stopped against your will
triggers: \bwouldn'?t let me (?:leave|go|out)\b|\bnot let me (?:leave|go|out)\b|\bprevented me from leaving\b|\bsurrounded my car\b|\bforced me to stay\b
playbooks.intro: Stopping someone from going where they have a right to go is wrongful restraint, and holding them within limits is wrongful confinement.

laws.why: Obstructing a person so they cannot go in a direction they have a right to go.
Restraining a person so they cannot go beyond certain limits, for example locking them in a room or shop.
If threats were made to make you do something.

steps.text: If you feel unsafe, call 112, even from inside the place where you are held.
Record names, numbers and the time. If you can, take photos or video, and note any CCTV.
Report it at any police station. It is recorded, read back and signed by you, and you get a copy free of cost.
If the police refuse, send the substance in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.

examples: my shop owner locked me in the store room
they would not let me leave until I signed the paper
a group surrounded my car and wouldn't let me go
the security guard stopped me from leaving the building

playbooks.title: Fire, vandalism or damage to property
playbooks.intro: Deliberately damaging or burning someone's property is mischief, and fire is treated more seriously.

laws.why: Intentionally causing wrongful loss or damage by destroying or reducing the value of property.
Mischief by fire or explosive substance, which carries a higher punishment.

steps.text: If there is a fire or danger, call 101 (fire) or 112 and get everyone to safety.
Photograph and video the damage and the area before anything is cleared. Note any CCTV or witnesses.
Tell your insurer, if you have a policy, and keep repair estimates and bills.
Report it to the police. It is recorded, read back and signed by you, and you get a copy free of cost.
If the police refuse, send it in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.

examples: someone set my bike on fire
my neighbour broke my car window on purpose
someone vandalised my shop
they burnt our crops

playbooks.title: Rape or sexual assault
playbooks.intro: This is a serious crime and it is never the victim's fault. Your safety and medical care come first, and you do not have to decide everything today.

laws.why: Defines rape.
Punishment for rape: rigorous imprisonment of not less than ten years, which may extend to life, and fine.
Higher punishment when the woman is under sixteen.
If more than one person was involved (gang rape).
If the offence was an assault or force intended to outrage her modesty rather than rape.

steps.text: If you or someone is in danger right now, call 112. Women Helpline 181 and 1091 also work in many states. Go to a safe place with someone you trust.
If you can, avoid washing, changing clothes or cleaning up before a medical examination, because that can preserve evidence. If you already did, you can still report and be examined.
When a woman reports rape or an attempt, her information must be recorded by a woman police officer. You can ask for one.
You can report at any police station, in any area, orally or electronically. It is read back to you and you sign it.
You are entitled to a copy of the recorded information, free of cost.

The medical examination is done by a registered medical practitioner, in a government hospital where possible, with your consent, and you must be sent for it within twenty-four hours of the information being received.
Ask about the victim compensation scheme and about support for rehabilitation.
If you fear threats, ask about the witness protection scheme.
Free legal aid and a lawyer are available from the District Legal Services Authority (NALSA helpline 15100). Counselling is available through Tele-MANAS 14416.

gather: A trusted person to go with you
Messages, call logs, photos of the place
Name or description of the person
playbooks.outside: If the victim is under 18, the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 also applies. It is not part of this tool. Childline 1098 can help.
examples: I was raped by someone I know
my friend was sexually assaulted
he forced himself on me

playbooks.title: Filing a police complaint (FIR)
playbooks.intro: Anyone can report a crime. The law lets you do it at any police station and even electronically.

laws.why: Information about a cognizable (serious) offence: how it is given, recorded and what you are entitled to.
For non-cognizable (usually minor) offences the police only record the information and refer you to the Magistrate.

steps.text: Note down what happened, when, where, who was involved and any witnesses. Keep screenshots, bills and photos together.
Go to any police station, whichever area the offence happened in, and give the information orally or by electronic communication.
If you give it orally, the police write it down, read it back to you, and you sign it.
If you send it electronically, it is taken on record once you sign it within three days.
Ask for a copy. It must be given to you free of cost. Keep the FIR number.
If the offence is non-cognizable, the police record the information and refer you to the Magistrate, and cannot investigate without the Magistrate's order.
If the police refuse to record a cognizable offence, send the substance in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.

examples: how do I file an FIR
can I file a police complaint online
where should I report a crime that happened in another city
how to report a crime to the police

playbooks.title: Police asking you to come in or answer questions
playbooks.intro: Being called to the police station is not the same as being arrested. What you must do depends on whether you are a witness or someone they suspect.

laws.why: The police can require a person who knows the facts to attend by an order in writing. Women, men under fifteen or over sixty, and disabled or acutely ill persons cannot be required to attend anywhere except their home.
For a suspect, the police must issue a notice to appear instead of arresting when arrest is not needed. If you comply, you are not to be arrested unless the officer records reasons.
If you are arrested and interrogated, you may meet an advocate of your choice during interrogation.

steps.text: Ask for the request in writing and ask whether you are being called as a witness or as a suspect. Note the officer's name and the case.

As a witness, you can be required to attend by a written order. If you are a woman, under fifteen, over sixty, disabled or acutely ill, you can ask to be questioned at your residence. You may also choose to go to the station.
As a suspect, you should get a written notice to appear. It is your duty to comply, and if you comply you are not to be arrested for that offence unless the officer records reasons.
Speak to a lawyer before you go, and take a relative or friend with you. If you cannot afford a lawyer, free legal aid is available from the District Legal Services Authority (NALSA helpline 15100).
If you are arrested and interrogated, you are entitled to meet your advocate during interrogation.
Do not sign anything you have not read. Keep a copy of the notice.

gather: A relative or friend who can come with you
examples: police called me to the station for questioning
I got a notice from the police asking me to appear
the police want my statement as a witness

playbooks.title: Falsely accused, or a case filed against you
playbooks.intro: Being accused is not the same as being guilty. The law gives you ways to avoid unnecessary arrest, to get bail and to challenge a case that has no basis.

laws.why: If arrest is not necessary, the police must give you a notice to appear instead of arresting you.
Advance (anticipatory) bail if you expect to be arrested for a non-bailable offence.
If you are arrested, you must be told the grounds and, for a bailable offence, that you can get bail.
The High Court's inherent power to prevent abuse of the process of any court. Lawyers use it to ask for a baseless case to be quashed.
Making a criminal charge you know to be false, with intent to injure someone, is itself an offence.

steps.text: Stay calm. Do not threaten, pressure or contact the person who complained, because that can be treated as intimidation and hurt your case.
Get a lawyer early. If you cannot afford one, free legal aid is available from the District Legal Services Authority (NALSA helpline 15100).
Collect evidence that supports you: messages, call records, bills, photos, CCTV locations and people who can confirm where you were.
If the police send a notice to appear, comply with it. If you comply, you are not to be arrested for that offence unless the officer records reasons.
If you fear arrest for a non-bailable offence, your lawyer can apply to the High Court or Court of Session for anticipatory bail.
If you are arrested, ask for the grounds of arrest. For a bailable offence you must be told you can get bail.
If the case is plainly baseless, your lawyer can ask the High Court to quash it.
If the charge is shown to be knowingly false, the person who made it can be prosecuted.

gather: Copy of the FIR or complaint (ask your lawyer to get it)
Your evidence: messages, call logs, bills, CCTV, witnesses
playbooks.outside: If the accusation is in a family dispute, related civil cases (divorce, maintenance, custody) are outside this tool.
examples: my wife's family filed a false dowry case against me
I was falsely accused of theft by my employer
someone filed a fake FIR against me
I am being framed for a crime I didn't commit

playbooks.title: Missing person or kidnapping
playbooks.intro: Report a missing person, especially a child, to the police at once. You do not have to wait before reporting.

laws.why: Taking or enticing a child (under eighteen) out of the keeping of the lawful guardian without consent is kidnapping.
Abduction: forcing or deceiving any person into going from a place.
Kidnapping or abduction for ransom, or to murder, carries a much higher punishment.

steps.text: Call 112 now. For a missing child you can also call Childline 1098. You do not need to wait 24 hours.
Give the police a recent photo, what the person was wearing, where and when they were last seen, their phone number and any social media accounts.
Check with friends, school or workplace, and nearby hospitals. Keep your phone on and note every call or message.
Report at any police station, whichever area it happened in. The information is written down, read back and signed by you, and you get a copy free of cost.
If someone demands ransom, tell the police before paying anything and keep every message and call record.
If the police refuse to record it, send the substance in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.

gather: Description, clothes, last seen time and place
Phone number, social media, friends' contacts
examples: my child has been missing since this morning
my cousin was kidnapped
my daughter hasn't come home from school
someone abducted my brother and wants ransom

playbooks.title: Police violence or misconduct in custody
playbooks.intro: Police are not allowed to hurt anyone to get a confession or information. The law requires a medical examination and production before a Magistrate.

laws.why: Causing hurt to extort a confession or information. The section's own illustration is a police officer torturing someone to make them confess.
An arrested person must be medically examined and the injuries recorded. A copy of the report goes to the person or their nominee.
No one can be kept in police custody beyond twenty-four hours without being produced before a Magistrate.

steps.text: Get medical treatment as soon as possible and photograph the injuries. Keep the reports.
If the person is in custody, insist on the medical examination after arrest and ask for a copy of the report.
When produced before the Magistrate, tell the Magistrate about the injuries and how they were caused.
Send a written complaint by post to the Superintendent of Police.
You can also apply to the Magistrate with an affidavit for an investigation to be ordered.
You can complain to the State Human Rights Commission or the National Human Rights Commission. Free legal aid: NALSA helpline 15100.

gather: Medical reports and photos of injuries
Names or badge numbers of the officers, station, date and time
playbooks.outside: Complaints to Human Rights Commissions are under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, which is not part of this tool.
examples: the cops beat me in custody
police tortured my brother at the station
the police hit my father during questioning

playbooks.title: Police seized your property
playbooks.intro: Police can seize property connected with an offence, but they must report it and you can apply to get it back.

laws.why: Police may seize property suspected to be stolen or linked to an offence, and must report the seizure to the Magistrate.
When seized property is not produced in court, the Magistrate can order it delivered to the person entitled to it.
When property is before a court, the court can order its custody while the case goes on, for example handing it back on a bond.

steps.text: Ask for the seizure memo (a list of what was taken) and the case or FIR number. Do not sign a list that is wrong.
The officer must report the seizure to the Magistrate. Property can be given to a person on a bond to produce it when required.
Apply to the Magistrate for release, with proof that you own it.
If the property is already before a court, apply to that court for interim custody.
A lawyer can file the release application. Free legal aid: NALSA helpline 15100.

examples: police seized my car and are not returning it
how do I get my phone back from the police
the police confiscated my documents

playbooks.title: Defamation or false rumours about you
playbooks.intro: Harming someone's reputation with false statements can be criminal defamation, but it is taken up on your complaint to a Magistrate, not as a regular police FIR.

laws.why: Making or publishing an imputation intending or knowing that it will harm a person's reputation. The section lists exceptions, such as true statements made for the public good.
A court takes up defamation only on a complaint by the person defamed (or, in some cases, someone on their behalf).
Defamation is non-cognizable, so the police only record the information and refer you to the Magistrate.

steps.text: Keep evidence: screenshots with date and time, links, the names of people who heard or saw it.
For online posts, report the post to the platform as well.
File a complaint before the Magistrate yourself, as the person defamed. A lawyer usually drafts it.
If you go to the police, they record it and refer you to the Magistrate. They cannot investigate without the Magistrate's order.
Talk to a lawyer about whether a legal notice or a civil suit for damages suits you better.

gather: Names of people who received the statements
playbooks.outside: A civil suit for damages is a separate option and is outside this tool.
examples: someone is spreading false rumours about me
my relative is telling lies about me to everyone
someone posted false things about me online to ruin my reputation

playbooks.title: Someone harmed or killed an animal
playbooks.intro: Killing, poisoning or maiming an animal is an offence, whether it is your pet or not.

laws.why: Killing, poisoning, maiming or rendering useless any animal.

steps.text: Take the animal to a vet at once. If it died, ask the vet for a post-mortem report: it is the main evidence.
Photograph the animal, the place and anything left behind (food, poison). Note witnesses and CCTV.
Report it at any police station, orally or electronically. It is written down, read back and signed by you, and you get a copy free of cost.
If the police refuse to record it, send the substance in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.

playbooks.outside: Cruelty that is not killing or maiming falls under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, which is not part of this tool. Animal welfare groups can help.
examples: someone poisoned my dog
my neighbour killed my cat
someone beat a street dog to death

playbooks.title: Someone entered your home or property
playbooks.intro: Entering or staying on property in someone else's possession to intimidate, insult, annoy or commit an offence is criminal trespass. Entering a home is treated more seriously.

laws.why: Defines criminal trespass and house-trespass, and their punishment.
Lurking house-trespass or house-breaking, punished more seriously at night.

steps.text: If the person is still there or you feel unsafe, call 112. Do not confront them alone.
Note the date and time, photograph any damage, and keep CCTV and witness details.
Report it at any police station, orally or electronically. It is written down, read back and signed by you, and you get a copy free of cost.
If the police refuse to record it, send the substance in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.

gather: Proof that you live in or possess the property
playbooks.outside: Disputes about who owns land or a house are civil matters and outside this tool.
examples: someone entered my house without permission
my neighbour keeps entering my land
a man broke the lock and got into my flat

playbooks.title: Second marriage while still married
playbooks.intro: Marrying again while a husband or wife is alive, when that marriage is void, is an offence. It is taken up on a complaint by the person wronged.

laws.why: Marrying again while a husband or wife is living, where that second marriage is void for that reason.
A court takes up offences against marriage only on a complaint by the person aggrieved, such as the first spouse.

steps.text: Collect proof of your marriage (certificate, photos, invitation) and of the second marriage.
File a complaint before the Magistrate as the aggrieved spouse. A lawyer usually drafts it.
Free legal aid: District Legal Services Authority, NALSA helpline 15100.

playbooks.outside: Divorce, maintenance and property claims are family-law matters outside this tool.
examples: my husband married another woman without divorcing me
my wife married someone else while still married to me

playbooks.title: Noise, garbage or another public nuisance
playbooks.intro: An act that causes common injury, danger or annoyance to people living nearby or using a public way is a public nuisance. A Magistrate can order it removed.

laws.why: Defines public nuisance: an act causing common injury, danger or annoyance to people nearby or to those using a public right of way.
Public nuisance not covered by any other section is punishable with a fine of up to one thousand rupees.
An Executive Magistrate (for example the SDM) can order an unlawful obstruction or nuisance removed from a public place or way.

steps.text: If it is safe, ask the person to stop. Often that is enough.
Keep a record: dates, times, short videos or audio, photos of garbage or the blocked way, and neighbours who are also affected.
For loud noise at night, call the local police or 112. Loudspeakers are generally not allowed between 10 pm and 6 am.
Apply to the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (an Executive Magistrate) to order the nuisance or obstruction removed from the public place or way.
For garbage, sewage or drains, complain to your municipal corporation or panchayat as well.

gather: Copies of complaints to the police or municipality
playbooks.outside: Noise limits are set by the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, and garbage by municipal laws. Neither is part of this tool.
examples: my neighbour plays loud music every night
someone dumps garbage outside my house
the shopkeeper has blocked the lane with his goods

playbooks.title: Someone kept or misused your property or money
playbooks.intro: If someone was trusted with your property or money (lent, given for safekeeping, a business partner, a spouse's family holding your jewellery), or got it by mistake, and dishonestly keeps or uses it, that can be a criminal offence and not only a civil dispute.

laws.why: If you entrusted the property to them (lent it, gave it for repair or safekeeping, a business partner handling joint funds, in-laws holding a bride's jewellery) and they dishonestly keep or use it.
Dishonestly keeping or using someone's movable property, for example money credited to them by mistake that they refuse to return.

steps.text: Ask for it back in writing (a message or email is fine) and give a clear date. Keep the reply, or the lack of one.
Collect proof that it is yours and that they have it: bills, photos, chats, receipts, the transaction ID or a handover note.
For money sent to the wrong account, tell your bank at once and ask it to contact the receiving bank.
If they still refuse, report it at the police station. The information is written down, read back and signed by you, and you get a copy free of cost.
If the police say it is only a civil matter and refuse to record it, send the substance in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.

gather: Chats or emails about handing it over
Your written request and their reply
Transaction ID and bank statement, if money
playbooks.outside: Recovering money or property through a civil suit is a separate route and outside this tool. A lawyer can advise which suits your case.
examples: someone borrowed my laptop and won't return it
I transferred money to the wrong person and they refuse to return it
my employer won't return my original certificates
I gave my car to a friend and he is not giving it back
my business partner has been taking money from our company account
my in-laws are keeping my jewellery

playbooks.title: Someone is following you
playbooks.intro: If you are being followed right now, your safety comes first. Afterwards it can be reported, and repeated following of a woman is the offence of stalking.
triggers: \b(?:car|bike|motorcycle|scooter|vehicle|auto|truck|van|jeep|suv)\b.{0,40}\b(?:follow\w*|tail\w*|chas\w*)\b.{0,15}\b(?:me|us|my|our)\b|\b(?:follow\w*|tail\w*|chas\w*)\b.{0,10}\b(?:me|us|my car|our car|my bike)\b.{0,40}(?:\b(?:car|bike|motorcycle|scooter|vehicle|auto|truck|van|jeep|suv)\b|\b(?:since|for) (?:the last )?\d+|\bminutes?\b|\bmins?\b|\bright now\b|\ball the way\b)

laws.why: If a man repeatedly follows a woman, or tries to contact her despite clear disinterest, that is stalking.
If they blocked your way or stopped you from going where you had a right to go.
If they threatened you.

steps.text: Call 112 now. Say where you are, which way you are going and the vehicle number if you can see it.
Do not go home or to a quiet place. Keep moving towards a busy, well-lit area or straight to a police station. Keep doors locked and windows up.
Do not stop to confront them. If someone is with you, ask them to note the number plate, colour and model, or record a video.
Call a friend or family member and stay on the line until you are safe.
Once you are safe, report it at any police station. It is written down, read back and signed by you, and you get a copy free of cost.
If a woman reports stalking, her information must be recorded by a woman police officer.

gather: Names of anyone who saw it
examples: a car has been following me for 20 minutes
someone on a bike is following me home
a car kept chasing us on the highway

playbooks.title: Problem with an auto, cab or taxi driver
playbooks.intro: Demanding extra money under pressure, refusing to take you where agreed, or leaving you somewhere unsafe can be an offence. Your safety comes first; the fare dispute can be settled later.

laws.why: If the driver puts you in fear (of being hurt, stranded or harmed) to make you pay more, that is extortion.
Threatening to harm you, your belongings or your reputation to make you do something.
If the driver stops you from getting out or going where you have a right to go.
laws.when: \b(?:won'?t (?:stop|let me)|not let me|locked|refus\w* to stop|wouldn'?t stop)\b

laws.why: If a woman passenger faces lewd words, gestures or remarks.

steps.text: If you feel unsafe, call 112 now. Share your live location with someone you trust and stay on the phone.
Get to a busy, well-lit place before arguing. If it is safe, pay the normal fare and settle the rest later. Your safety matters more than the money.
Note the vehicle number, the driver's name and photo, the time and the route. Take a photo of the number plate if you can.
If you booked through an app (Ola, Uber, Rapido and others), use its safety or SOS button and report the driver in the app.
Overcharging and refusing a ride can also be reported to the traffic police or your state transport department.
If you were threatened or forced to pay, report it at any police station. It is written down, read back and signed by you, and you get a copy free of cost.
If the police refuse to record it, send it in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate.

gather: Vehicle number and photo of the number plate
playbooks.outside: Fares and refusals to ply are set by the Motor Vehicles Act and state fare rules, which are not part of this tool.
examples: auto driver is demanding more money to drop me
the cab driver left me at a random place
the taxi driver took a wrong route and is threatening me
an auto driver refused to stop and asked for double fare

generic.title: What to do after any offence
generic.intro: These steps apply to any crime. The sections below are the closest match to what you described, so read them to check they fit.

steps.text: If anyone is in danger or hurt, call 112 first.
Write down what happened: the date, time and place, who was involved and who saw it. Keep the evidence (photos, messages, documents, medical reports). Do not delete anything.
Report it at any police station, whichever area it happened in, orally or electronically. If oral, it is written down, read back to you and signed by you.
Ask for a copy of what was recorded. It must be given to you free of cost.
If the offence is non-cognizable (usually minor), the police record the information and refer you to the Magistrate. They cannot investigate without the Magistrate's order.
If the police refuse to record a cognizable offence, send the substance in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police.
You can also apply to the Magistrate, with an affidavit, who may order an investigation.
Free legal aid is available from your District Legal Services Authority (NALSA helpline 15100).

gather: A written timeline of what happened
ID proof and a copy of your complaint
